quote: Anziehung zweier flüssiger Kugeln (zwei Welt- körper) aus zwei getrennten Theilen bestehende Gleichgewichtsfiguren. Versuche durch Rotation einer Lemniskate.
english: Attraction of two fluid spheres (two celestial bodies); equilibrium figures consisting of two separate parts. Attempts by rotation of a lemniscate.
topic: Notes on series of rational functions representing analytic functions, the problem of rational parametrization of surfaces (solved by Castelnuovo in a special case), equilibrium figures of two rotating fluid masses, and Euler's view that impenetrability is the cause of all forces.

triage.modern_statement: Do rigidly rotating, self-gravitating fluid masses have equilibrium configurations made of two separate (disjoint) components, such as two fluid 'spheres' or celestial bodies held together by their mutual attraction? This is the binary-star or 'double star' equilibrium-figure problem: find steady solutions of the incompressible or compressible Euler–Poisson equations in a rotating frame whose support has two connected components. It also asks whether such figures are stable, and how they relate to single-body figures. Hilbert's 'attempt by rotating a lemniscate' suggests he tried a dumbbell-shaped trial surface (a surface of revolution generated by a lemniscate) as an ansatz bridging one-body and two-body figures. That reading of the lemniscate is an inference from the note itself, not something a source states.
triage.answered_by: The problem was treated approximately by G. H. Darwin, building on Roche and Jeans. Darwin's 1906 Royal Society memoir 'On the Figure and Stability of a Liquid Satellite' covered synchronously rotating homogeneous binary masses (Darwin ellipsoids). Chandrasekhar revisited it in 1964 in ApJ 140, 'The equilibrium and the stability of double-star systems'. Leon Lichtenstein gave rigorous existence results using integro-differential equations and successive approximations; these cover Roche satellites and liquid double stars with and without solid centres, and are collected in his monograph 'Gleichgewichtsfiguren rotierender Flüssigkeiten' (Berlin, 1933). A modern variational existence proof of stable, slowly and uniformly rotating binary stars with a prescribed mass ratio, whose fluid splits into two disjoint regions, was given by R. J. McCann, 'Stable rotating binary stars and fluid in a tube', Houston J. Math. (2006).

evidence.claim: Darwin's 1906 memoir treats the figure and stability of a liquid satellite, extending Roche's problem.

Chandrasekhar's 1964 ApJ paper on the equilibrium and stability of double-star systems names Darwin (1906) as the principal earlier work. It describes Darwin's problem as synchronously rotating homogeneous masses under their mutual gravitational and tidal interaction.

Lichtenstein's 1933 monograph builds integro-differential equations solved by successive approximations. It covers new problems including Roche's satellites and liquid double stars with and without solid centres.
Lichtenstein's work on rotating fluids is surveyed in a later chapter. He was professor in Leipzig from 1922 until his death in 1933.
McCann (2006) proves that stable, slowly and uniformly rotating binary stars exist with a specified mass ratio. In these solutions the fluid mass is split into two disjoint, widely separated regions.
Recent work on rotating-star existence cites McCann's binary stars and studies star–planet systems, so the area is still active.
A historical survey of the theory of equilibrium figures, covering Darwin's stability work from 1902–08 among other contributions.

triage.why: The note is short but clearly about two-component equilibrium figures of rotating, self-gravitating fluid. This classical problem was handled approximately by Roche, Darwin (1906) and Jeans, and later by Chandrasekhar (1964). Lichtenstein proved existence for liquid double stars rigorously (summarized in 1933), and McCann (2006) gave a modern variational existence and stability proof. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Work on rotating-star and binary-type solutions of the Euler–Poisson equations continues today, for example the 2026 arXiv paper on star models. The sources do not show that the lemniscate ansatz itself was ever pursued, and I could not date Hilbert's note precisely, so it is uncertain whether it came before Darwin or Lichtenstein. Confidence is medium for these reasons.
